jovial

/JOH-vee-ul/ — accent on first syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Jovial describes someone who is warm, cheerful, and full of good humor.

Our jovial neighbor greets everyone with a joke and a wave.

Example

The hospice nurse's jovial laugh and warm greeting made even the sickest patients smile and feel genuinely cared for.

The warmth here—the genuine cheerfulness that puts others at ease—is exactly what jovial captures. Because the greeting reflects deep warmth, not just friendliness, jovial is more precise than 'friendly.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

merry: Merry means full of lively, festive cheer, and it usually belongs to occasions and moments — a merry party, a merry laugh at dinner. Jovial belongs to the person: warm, hearty good humor someone carries everywhere, party or no party. The evening is merry; the host is jovial.

affable: Affable means easy to talk to and approachable — an affable person makes conversation comfortable without necessarily being funny or festive. Jovial goes further: hearty cheer and good humor that actively warms a room. An affable clerk answers questions pleasantly; a jovial one leaves you grinning.

convivial: Convivial means merry and sociable, loving good company — a convivial person is happiest sharing food, talk, and long evenings with others, and the word fits festive gatherings too. Jovial is about humor: the warm, laughing good cheer of the person telling the jokes. Convivial loves the company; jovial supplies the laughter.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dour: stern, gloomy, and severe in manner

morose: gloomy, silent, and stubbornly bad-tempered

Where it sits · how much warmth and cheer radiates

polite → friendly → genial → jovial

polite vs. jovial: Polite is far weaker than jovial: a polite person simply follows good manners, while a jovial person radiates warmth, laughter, and hearty good humor.

friendly vs. jovial: Friendly is warmer than polite but still weaker than jovial — a friendly person is pleasant to be around, while a jovial one actively fills the whole room with cheer.

genial vs. jovial: Genial comes close to jovial, but jovial is stronger: a genial host is warmly agreeable, while a jovial host is bubbling over with jokes and merry laughter.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — Jov: Jove (Jupiter), the Roman sky god (Latin)

Suffix — -ial: characteristic of, pertaining to (Latin)

Put it together: Jov- names the Roman god Jove (Jupiter) and -ial means 'characteristic of' — astrologers believed people born under the planet Jupiter were blessed with merry, good-humored natures, so jovial literally means 'like Jove': warm and cheerful.

Use the root in a new word: Jovian: Jovian comes straight from Jove — Latin Jovis, the Roman sky god the Romans also called Jupiter. Romans believed people born under Jove's sign were the luckiest of all, and that merry good-luck reputation is exactly where jovial gets its cheer. Jovian, though, is a word you are far more likely to meet in a science classroom than in a horoscope.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Jovial is the warmth that spreads — reach for it when someone's cheer is genuine, infectious, and makes others feel included. For simple friendliness or politeness, 'friendly' is simpler.
